Workspaces and task rows

Workspace tabs were easiest to identify, while the labeled bottom shelf kept one more complete task on screen. Try both with the same aligned Notes editor and Adaptive spacing. The two buttons change only workspace navigation.

Every option uses compact date chips, spelled-out trailing deadlines, a checked active workspace and a scheduled value before the expanded task’s completion circle.

Switching workspaces

All three follow-up reviewers gave the persistent tabs 10/10. They show the destination before the first tap and cost 40 pt of list height. The bottom shelf scored 9.50/10 and keeps the full list height when closed. Its second tap comes at the cost of temporarily replacing date and capture. Moving the chooser above the footer preserved those controls but scored 9.33: it covered task text and repeated the active workspace name. With Adaptive spacing, the tabs show 16 complete rows at 390 pt; the bottom shelf shows 17.

Expanded task controls

Use the card width for the controls and compare where Notes starts. The first panel favored the full-width strip but all three reviewers noticed the jump from the title to Notes. In the follow-up, all three gave 9.50/10 when Notes shared the title edge and only the chips moved left. All five chips fit in one line at 440 pt. At 390 pt the two dates wrap together. Two reviewers still found the 10:00 AM time close to the left card edge.

Row spacing

Balanced and Adaptive tied at 9.17/10 in the follow-up. Adaptive spends less height on a plain row and reserves space beneath a project tag. That fit 17 complete rows at 390 pt and 20 at 440 pt, one more at each width than Balanced. Tight fits one more row at 390 pt, but all three reviewers found either tag-to-title gaps or the expanded card edges cramped. One reviewer still preferred the extra separation around tags in Balanced.

How the options were compared

Nine independent Codex GPT-6.2-astra sessions at high reasoning effort reviewed shuffled, anonymously identified screenshot sheets. Three reviewers first scored the modeled references. Three fresh reviewers then compared ten options. Three more scored eight options in a follow-up, including exact copies of the previous tabs, shelf, full-width editor, Tight and Balanced sheets. Scores are means out of ten. Each sheet contributes equally within its decision. A dash in the table means the option was absent from that panel.

Initial reference scores were 8.33 for navigation, 8.67 for editor placement and 8.33 for spacing. Compare options within a panel. Reference scores moved when other designs were present. Each reviewer scored orientation, scanability, affordance, legibility and composition from zero to two in half-point steps. The raw file preserves all 63 ballots and comments.

The benchmark uses a fixed 28-row Planner fixture with short and wrapped titles, projects, timed and untimed work, and three relative deadlines. App chrome is taken from iPhone 18 Pro Max XCUITest screenshots at 4fe70da. Rows, destinations, controls and menus are browser prototypes. The benchmark reference models the approved choices over that chrome. Each axis was varied independently against the other two references. The combined prototype is available for inspection and has no aggregate reviewer score.

Navigation images show the starting view, available choices and arrival at 440 × 956 pt. Editor sheets show the same task collapsed and expanded at 440 pt, then expanded at 390 pt. Density sheets use 390 × 844 pt, both collapsed and expanded. We also measured visible rows and expanded card heights at both widths. A row counts only when its entire bounding box fits between the header and reserved footer. Automated checks exercised all 80 layout combinations at both sizes and confirmed the five chips fit within the card and the resting footer controls do not overlap.

These are light-appearance, standard-text studies. Thumb reach, native gestures, touch accuracy, larger text and VoiceOver were outside this test. Taps refer to the modeled path between top-level workspaces. Raster comparison found the first reference menu sheet differed by 58 of 1,327,872 pixels on re-render; the editor and spacing references matched pixel for pixel. Follow-up repeat sheets reused the exact earlier images.
